paragraphs: What we have just said confirms Chapter XVI. It makes clear that the institution of government is not a contract but a law. The holders of the executive power are not the people’s masters but its officers. The people can appoint them and remove them whenever it likes. For them there is no question of contract, only of obedience. In taking on the functions the State assigns them, they do no more than fulfill their duty as citizens, and they have not the slightest right to argue about the conditions.

When the people, therefore, sets up a hereditary government, whether monarchical and confined to one family, or aristocratic and confined to one class, it is not making a commitment. It is giving the administration a provisional form, until the people chooses to order it otherwise.

It is true that such changes are always dangerous, and that an established government should never be touched except when it becomes incompatible with the public good. But the caution this requires is a maxim of policy, not a rule of right. The State is no more bound to leave civil authority in the hands of its rulers than to leave military authority in the hands of its generals.

It is also true that one cannot be too careful, in such cases, to observe all the formalities needed to tell a regular and legitimate act from a seditious riot, and the will of a whole people from the clamor of a faction. Here above all, no more should be conceded to the unfavorable possibility than cannot, by the strictest logic, be refused it. The prince draws a great advantage from this obligation in keeping his power against the people without it being possible to say that he has usurped it. For while he seems to be using only his rights, he finds it very easy to extend them. Under the pretext of keeping the peace, he can prevent the assemblies that are meant to restore order. He takes advantage of a silence he does not allow to be broken, or of irregularities he himself causes, to assume that he has the support of those whom fear keeps from speaking, and to punish those who dare to speak. This is how the decemvirs, first elected for one year and then kept in office for a second, tried to make their power permanent by forbidding the comitia to assemble. And by this easy method every government in the world, once clothed with public power, sooner or later usurps the sovereign authority.

The periodic assemblies I have already spoken of are meant to prevent or postpone this calamity, above all when they need no formal summons. In that case the prince cannot stop them without openly declaring himself a lawbreaker and an enemy of the State.

The sole purpose of these assemblies is to maintain the social treaty. Their opening should always take the form of putting two propositions, which may not be suppressed and which should be voted on separately.
The first is: “Does it please the Sovereign to preserve the present form of government?”
The second is: “Does it please the people to leave its administration in the hands of those who are actually in charge of it?”

Here I am assuming what I think I have shown: that there is in the State no fundamental law that cannot be revoked, not even the social compact itself. For if all the citizens assembled and agreed together to break the compact, it is impossible to doubt that it would be broken quite legitimately. Grotius even thinks that each man can renounce his membership in his own State, and recover his natural liberty and his goods when he leaves the country.[1] It would be absurd indeed if all the citizens together could not do what each of them can do alone.
